# AGENTS.md

Notes for any agent working in this repo. The owner's direction is written here so it survives between sessions. Read it before changing the skill, the kit, a plan or the site.

## What this repo is

Blueprint: an agent skill (`skills/blueprint/`) that generates parametric build plans for anything a workshop makes, as one standalone HTML page per plan. Also `skills/blueprint-share/` (opens a PR that adds someone's plan here), `skills/blueprint/examples/` (the official examples, shipped with the skill and shown on the site), `plans/` (plans people share), and `tools/site.mjs` (the GitHub Pages site: a landing page plus every plan and its guide).

## How it should look and read: an IKEA guide

The full rules are in `skills/blueprint/references/kit.md` ("How the page looks"); in short:

- **Clear above all.** If it does not help someone build the thing, remove it.
- **Generated, not hand-made.** Every drawing, table, figure and number comes from a plan's `design.mjs` through the kit. New figures are generators in `kit/shop.mjs`, never hand-drawn SVG or HTML.
- **Space, not boxes.** Sections ~144 px apart, steps ~112 px, step numbers 64 px bold. No rules or boxed panels between them.
- **Minimal elements.** Black ink on white paper, never a dark theme. No shadows, gradients or decorative borders. Icons only where they mean something: ✓ check, ! warning, circled ? explainer, open-in-new-tab, printer.
- **Colour is a code** (`CODE` in `kit/shop.mjs`): yellow = look here (new in this step, help), green = the check, red = the warning (and the clicked part in 3D). Everything else black and white.
- **Minimal text.** Short imperative tasks. Teaching goes in the plan's guide (`guide.html`), reached through the `?` explainers.
- **No header of any kind.** No bar, nav, logo or version line, nothing pinned to the top or its corners. A plan opens with its title, then the 3D model and its fields, then the numbered Contents list with dotted leaders (in a card, its heading inside), then the start-here link. A guide opens with its title, then the same Contents card. The landing page opens on "Blueprint" and its tagline.
- **Labels on drawings** in white boxes. **The 3D model** in the anatomy style.
- **Phone and paper.** 16 px gutter, no sideways scroll at 390 px, print styles hide controls.
- **Metric by default**, imperial when asked; an mm / in switch on every plan.

## Engineering rules

- Every plan must pass its audit at every size its fields allow, and its capture: `node skills/blueprint/scripts/blueprint.mjs check plans/<id>/design.mjs`. Fix the design, never a check.
- After any change to the page, the guide or the site, capture every example: its layout audit must be clean (numbers, checkboxes, marks and icons within 1 px of their text, measured on the ink). Look at screenshots too, but trust the measurements.
- After a kit change, keep green: `blueprint.mjs test`, the audit of every plan and example, `node tools/site.mjs`, and the capture of each example. Existing plans should build to the same checks unless the change means to move them.
- After changing a `SKILL.md` or a reference: `python -m skills_ref.cli validate skills/blueprint` (and `blueprint-share`) must pass, and the scenarios in `skills/blueprint/evals/evals.json` should still pass with a fresh agent.
- The official examples live only in `skills/blueprint/examples/`; `plans/` is only for shared plans. Never keep a second copy of a plan.
- Plans contributed through `blueprint-share` add exactly one file, `plans/<id>/design.mjs`.

## Writing style

Plain words, no em dashes. Terse in the plan, explanatory only in the guide.

## Git

Work on a branch, open a PR when asked, and check whether the previous PR was already merged before pushing more commits to it (start a new branch from `main` if so).

# Blueprint share

Turns a plan made with the `blueprint` skill into a pull request on [pham-tuan-binh/blueprint](https://github.com/pham-tuan-binh/blueprint). Once it is merged, the site builds the plan into its own page and puts a card for it on the landing page, credited to its author. Nothing else in the repo changes: a plan is one file, `plans/<id>/design.mjs`.

`$SHARE` below is the folder this SKILL.md is in, and `$SKILL` is the `blueprint` skill's folder (usually its sibling); write them out in full.

## What gets merged

- **Exactly one file**: `plans/<id>/design.mjs`. Not `index.html`, not `shots/`: CI builds the page from the design, and screenshots are for the author's review only.
- **It passes the audit with the repo's kit.** CI audits every plan on every pull request, so a plan that fails there cannot merge. The share script runs the same audit before anything is pushed.
- **It credits its author**: `author: { github: 'handle', name: 'Name' }` on the plan, right after `summary`. The card says "by @handle".
- **Its id is new**: lower-case words joined by dashes, not already in `plans/` or the skill's examples.
- **Its summary reads as a card description**: one or two sentences, under 320 characters, saying what it is and how it is built. It is all a visitor reads before they open it.
- It is something a person can build in a workshop, made with the skill, not a copy of an example with the numbers changed.

## Workflow

1. **Check the plan first.** It must pass the blueprint skill's full check, browser included:
   `node $SKILL/scripts/blueprint.mjs check plans/<id>/design.mjs`
   If it does not pass, fix it with the blueprint skill before going on. Read the shots: what you share is what everyone sees.
2. **Add the author** to the plan if it is not there. Ask the person for their GitHub handle; do not guess it.
   ```js
   summary: '…',
   author: { github: 'their-handle', name: 'Their Name' },
   ```
3. **Fork and clone the repo** (once). With the GitHub CLI:
   ```bash
   gh auth status || gh auth login
   gh repo fork pham-tuan-binh/blueprint --clone     # makes ./blueprint, with origin = their fork
   ```
   Without it, have the person fork on github.com (the Fork button), then `git clone https://github.com/<handle>/blueprint`. If they already have a clone, bring it up to date: `git -C blueprint pull https://github.com/pham-tuan-binh/blueprint main`.
4. **Run the share script.** It copies the plan in, audits it with the repo's kit, builds the site to confirm the page and card appear, and writes the PR text:
   ```bash
   node $SHARE/scripts/share.mjs plans/<id>/design.mjs --repo blueprint
   ```
   It must end with `ready.` and print the next commands. Exit 1 means the plan fails in the repo: fix it with the blueprint skill and run it again. If the audit passes locally but fails here, the repo's kit is newer than the installed skill: update the skill (`npx skills add pham-tuan-binh/blueprint`) and recheck. Updating a plan you shared before: add `--update`.
5. **Show the person what will be sent** (the file and the PR text) and get their go-ahead. A pull request is public.
6. **Branch, commit, push and open the PR** with the commands the script printed:
   ```bash
   cd blueprint
   git checkout -b plan/<id>
   git add plans/<id>/design.mjs
   git commit -m "Add plan: <name>"
   git push -u origin plan/<id>
   gh pr create --repo pham-tuan-binh/blueprint --head <handle>:plan/<id> --title "Add plan: <name>" --body-file .git/blueprint-pr-<id>.md
   ```
   Without gh: open the fork on github.com, "Contribute" > "Open pull request", and paste the PR text.
7. **Tell the person** the PR link, that CI audits it and builds the site, and the address it will have once merged: `https://pham-tuan-binh.github.io/blueprint/<id>/`. If CI fails, read the failing step's log, fix the plan, and push to the same branch.

## Rules

- Never push to `pham-tuan-binh/blueprint` itself or to its `main`: always a branch on the person's fork, then a pull request.
- Never change anything outside `plans/<id>/` in a share PR (not the kit, not the site, not another plan). A kit fix is a separate PR with its own reason.
- Never edit a check or loosen a field range to get a plan through the audit; fix the design.
- Never commit, push or open the PR before the person has seen what will be sent.

# Blueprint

You write one file, `plans/<id>/design.mjs`: params plus a pure `build(p, k)` that returns the model. The kit turns it into the page (3D view, checks, materials, prints, drawings, steps, cut list) and a guide beside it. Every plan gets the same sections, drawings, checks and look; your job is the design.

`$SKILL` is the folder this file is in (`doctor` prints it); write it out in full. Run the scripts, never read them to use them: `blueprint.mjs help` lists every command and flag.

```bash
node $SKILL/scripts/blueprint.mjs doctor                                   # first: what this machine lacks, and the fix
node $SKILL/scripts/blueprint.mjs examples                                 # the examples and what each shows
node $SKILL/scripts/blueprint.mjs new <id> --from <example> --name "Name"  # plans/<id>/design.mjs from an example
node $SKILL/scripts/blueprint.mjs check plans/<id>/design.mjs              # build + audit + browser capture: "check passed"
```

`check` stops at the first failing stage. Exit 0 passed, 1 a check failed (fix the design), 2 bad usage or a missing tool (run `doctor`). `--hash "top=steel"` (repeatable) also captures a variant. With no browser: `--no-browser`, and tell the user the page was not opened. Never skip the audit. A file from `new` carries a "STARTED FROM" note; the audit fails until you have rewritten the plan and deleted it.

## Examples

Open the closest one and copy its shape.

| Example | Shows |
|---|---|
| `shelf-rack` | the smallest plan: posts with `prio`, a limit that follows another field, notched decks, a plan check, an anchored tip check |
| `metal-workbench` | a design that adapts (middle legs, rail spacing), a `bool`, four load cases, bars placed by a rule, foot plates, `{mark:id}` |
| `pvc-drying-stand` | bought fittings with real shapes, pipes cut to the socket, a load limit that follows size, a stance check |
| `v-dipole-137` | 3D prints (solids, cuts, `bed`, copies) kept quick to print, non-steel materials, electrical plan checks, coax routed inside the mast, a two-part wind load |

## The rule: the model is the plan

Every length, angle, coordinate, quantity and mass is computed in `build(p, k)`, never written into prose. Text formats sizes with `k.u` (`u.len(mm)`, `u.len(mm, { u: true })`, `u.fine`, `u.size`, `u.mass`, `u.tol`). If a number appears, it was computed. Every step says what to cut, where it goes, how it is held and the check before the next step.

## Workflow

When you build a plan, copy this checklist into your reply and tick it off as you go (not when step 1 says not to build it):

```
Plan progress:
- [ ] 1. Size it (Part / Assembly / Machine)
- [ ] 2. Truth first: loads, ground, place, tools, stock
- [ ] 3. Structure and materials, in words
- [ ] 4. design.mjs started with `new --from`, then written
- [ ] 5. `check` passes (fix, rerun, until "check passed")
- [ ] 6. Every PNG read, references/verify.md answered
- [ ] 7. Delivered with numbers and assumptions
```

1. **Size it.** A *Part* (one frame, up to ~40 members): build it. An *Assembly* (sub-assemblies or moving parts, 40-120 members): say so, build it. A *Machine* is anything that carries people, lifts loads overhead, moves under power, or goes on a public road (a trailer, even towed and unbraked, is one): do not build it, however simple it looks. Say what it would need (an engineer's sign-off, the standard or road rules that govern it, a proof load test) and offer the Part or Assembly that keeps the core (a stand, a dolly, a yard cart), built only if the user takes it.
2. **Truth first.** Write down the loads and how they act, what it stands on, where it lives, the builder's tools, the stock they can buy. Ask only if the answer changes the design; otherwise choose common local stock and say so.
3. **Structure and materials.** Pick each material for what the job asks of it (load, weather, weight, whether it conducts, the builder's tools), not by habit; the materials files (below) say what each is good at. Describe the design in words first: how load gets from where it is applied to the ground, how each part joins, what runs through it, and the order it goes together.
4. **Write `design.mjs`** with `new --from`: params, then sections, nodes, members, plates, hardware, prints, supports, loads, tip, plan checks, steps.
5. **Check it, fix it, check again** until it ends `check passed`. `audit <design.mjs> --at "length=800"` prints every check at one size, for a closer look at a failure or a threshold. Each failure names the stage, the size and the check. Fix the design, never a check: a weak member gets a bigger section or a brace, a failing size gets a design that adapts, a hard-coded "mm" gets `u.len()`. Capture every `choice` option and every size where the design changes with `--hash`.
6. **Verify like a builder**: read every PNG in `shots/`, then go through [references/verify.md](references/verify.md). A no sends you back to step 5.
7. **Deliver** the plan folder (`design.mjs`, `index.html`, `guide.html`, `shots/` with the printed pack `plan.pdf`) with the size, the main numbers (mass, load and safety factor, cost), your assumptions about stock and load, and how to change the size (the fields; the URL keeps it). To publish it on the plans site, use the `blueprint-share` skill.

Put plans in `plans/<id>/` in the user's project, never inside the skill folder.

## Rules

These hold for anything a workshop makes. Ask each one of every part, joint and step; the references show how it plays out for frames, prints, pipe and wiring, but the rule decides. In order of impact: the first six break a plan, the rest make it hard to build from.

- **Parametric.** Fields for the sizes a person would change (length, width, height, plus what they mentioned), 5-8 typical and fewer for a small part, each with `min`, `max` and a common default. Every check must pass at every size the fields allow. A limit may follow earlier fields (`max: p => ...`). When a size needs more structure, make the design add it (`if (p.length > 1800) ...`) instead of narrowing the field. Narrow a field only at a hard limit the design cannot move (the printer bed, the stock length, the thing stops making sense), and say so in its hint.
- **Prove it does its job.** Name every way it can fail (break, bend, tip, slip, loosen, leak, detune, overheat) and give each a check at its worst size. Loads: one case for the job at its rating, placed where it does most harm, and one for the abuse a person or the weather will really give it. Safety factor 2 on strength for what holds things, 3 for anything a person stands on, sits on or hangs from. What is not a load (a length, a clearance, a current) is a plan check.
- **Every part can be made and fitted, in order.** Walk the steps with each part in hand: can it be made with the builder's tools, pass what is already built, and be reached to fasten it? Work that heats, dirties or shakes comes before what it would spoil. If the order cannot work, change the design, not the words.
- **Everything that runs through it has a route.** Cables, hoses, pipes, water and air: trace each from end to end. Inside a hollow member when there is one, in and out through a real hole or open end, its connectors reachable when that step comes, nothing pinching it, and water out at a low point. A route left for the builder to improvise is a missing part.
- **Every part is in a step and on the materials list.** Plates, feet, bolts, paint, wire.
- **Size each part to its job.** Mass, cost, print hours and work all follow size, so nothing is bigger, deeper, thicker or denser than a check needs. Stack features rather than spreading them, and pick the lightest stock that passes. When one part takes most of the mass, cost or time in its table, rethink that part first.
- **Simple to make.** The fewest operations the builder's tools allow: straight pieces, square cuts, one or two stock sizes, joints that repeat. A bend, cope, notch or a mitre between different sections only when asked. The load takes the direct path: what carries most runs through, the rest butts onto it, never onto anything smaller (frames: `references/structure.md`).
- **Units.** Metric unless the user asks for imperial (`units: 'imperial'`, imperial stock via `k.inch()`, round inch defaults). The model is always mm; stock never depends on the display units. Bought parts keep their trade names.
- **Name for the builder.** Plain member names, readable node names (`FL0`), pieces by mark in text (`{mark:member-id}`). Members that share a mark share a name.
- **Model what it looks like.** Bought fittings and prints take their real shape (`k.shapes`, or your own mesh).
- **Tolerances a person can hold** (±1 mm cuts, diagonals within 2-3 mm), with how to check them. **Honest about limits**: if it only passes anchored or braced, say so in the check and the step.
- **Short text.** Imperative tasks, no teaching (the guide's `?` explainers do that). Plain words, no em dashes.

## Done when

- `check` ends `check passed` (with `--hash` for every option and every size where the design changes), or `--no-browser` and the user is told.
- Every question in [references/verify.md](references/verify.md) is a yes.
- No number in the plan's text was typed by hand, and no "STARTED FROM" note is left.
- The user has the folder, the main numbers and your assumptions.

# Shared plans

Plans people made with the blueprint skill and shared with the `blueprint-share` skill. Each is one file, `plans/<id>/design.mjs`; CI audits it at every size its fields allow, and the site builds it into its own page with a card on the landing page.

The official examples live in `skills/blueprint/examples/`, inside the skill, so they install with it; the site shows them too.

# The kit, and how the page must look

Read this only when you change the kit (`kit/`, `scripts/`). A plan never imports the kit: `build(p, k)` gets the helpers in `k`, and the build script bundles kit and design into one page.

## Files

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `scripts/blueprint.mjs` | The one command: `doctor`, `examples`, `new`, `build`, `audit`, `capture`, `check`, `test`. The other scripts are its stages. |
| `scripts/build.mjs` | `design.mjs` to one standalone `index.html` (sections pre-rendered, so it reads and prints without JavaScript) and `guide.html`. |
| `scripts/audit.mjs` | Every check at every size the fields allow, and the plan lint. Prints `audit passed`. |
| `scripts/capture.mjs` | The page in headless Chromium: fields, units, 3D view, downloads (every STL watertight at every end of every field), guide, phone width, the layout audit (`scripts/layout.mjs`), screenshots, `--pdf`. Prints `capture passed`. |
| `scripts/env.mjs` | Finds Node, Playwright, Chromium and pdftoppm for `doctor` and `capture`. |
| `scripts/test-fea.mjs` | The frame solver against textbook beams. |
| `kit/core.mjs` | Vectors, materials, stock sections with their properties, metric and imperial formatters, params with dynamic limits. |
| `kit/shapes.mjs` | Mesh generators (`k.shapes`): sphere, cone, sweep, arc, bend, revolve, extrude. |
| `kit/print.mjs` | 3D prints: boxes, filament and time, bed turn, the exact solid (`printManifold`, manifold-3d: always watertight), the STL, the OpenSCAD source (same facets as the STL). |
| `kit/joints.mjs` | The joint solver: through, mitre, butt or flush at every node; each member trimmed to its real cut planes. |
| `kit/derive.mjs` | `derive(plan, params, units)`: joints, piece and plate marks, nesting, mass, analysis, tip-over, every check, cost, hours. |
| `kit/fea.mjs` | 3D beam frame solver. |
| `kit/shop.mjs` | SVG drawings: third-angle sheets, jigs, cut sheets, plate drawings, cutting plans; `CODE`, the colour code. |
| `kit/pack.mjs`, `kit/page.mjs` | The page sections and the HTML shell, print styles included. |

## How the page looks: an IKEA guide

- **Clear above all.** If it does not help someone build the thing, leave it out.
- **Generated, not hand-made.** Every drawing, table, number and figure comes from `design.mjs` through the kit. A missing figure is a new generator in `kit/shop.mjs`, never hand-written SVG or HTML in a plan.
- **Space, not boxes.** Sections ~144 px apart, steps ~112 px, step numbers 64 px bold. No rules or boxed panels between them.
- **Minimal elements.** Black ink on white paper, never a dark theme. No shadows, gradients or decorative borders. Icons only where they mean something, centred in their circle: ✓ check, ! warning, circled ? explainer, open-in-new-tab, printer.
- **Colour is a code** (`CODE` in `kit/shop.mjs`, the 3D view matches): yellow = look here (new in this step, help, start here), green = the ✓ check, red = the ! warning (and the clicked part in 3D). Everything else black, white and grey. No new colour without one meaning here.
- **Minimal text.** Short imperative tasks; teaching lives in the guide, reached through the `?` explainers.
- **No header of any kind.** No bar, nav, logo or version line, nothing pinned to the top or its corners. A plan opens with its title, then the 3D model and its fields, then a numbered Contents list with dotted leaders in a card (the word Contents inside it, lined up with the item titles), then the start-here link to the guide. Links and controls sit in the flow where a document would put them.
- **No lede, no facts grid.** The summary is for the gallery card; the totals are one line at the top of the materials list.
- **Say it once.** Nothing repeats what a field already shows: no line restating the sizes under the fields, no fact or check that only echoes an input (a check whose pass the field's min and max already guarantee is not a check).
- **Labels on drawings** in their own white boxes. **The 3D model** in the anatomy style: orthographic, four greys by face direction, thin outlines, one accent.
- **Phone and paper.** 16 px gutter, no sideways scroll at 390 px; print styles hide the controls and print the folded cut sheets open.
- **Metric by default**, imperial when asked; an mm / in switch on every plan.

# The design.mjs schema

Read this when writing `design.mjs`. `examples/shelf-rack/design.mjs` (in the skill folder) is the whole shape in about 150 lines: read it top to bottom first.

## Contents

- The plan object
- Units
- params: the input fields
- build(p, k): what `k` holds
- The model: members, plates, hardware, shapes, supports and loads, steps, checks
- A plan with no frame

## The plan object

A plan is one file that exports `plan` and imports nothing. `derive()` calls `plan.build(p, k)` on every input change, in Node for the audit and in the browser for the page, so `build` must be **pure**: same params, same model; no randomness, dates or network.

```js
export const plan = {
  id: 'metal-workbench',          // kebab-case; also the key for saved ticks on the page
  name: 'Welded steel workbench', // the page title
  version: '1',
  summary: 'One sentence: what it is, what it holds, how it is built.',   // the gallery card
  author: { github: 'handle', name: 'Name' },   // optional; needed to share it (blueprint-share)
  units: 'metric',                // or 'imperial' when the user asked for it
  currency: '$',                  // optional; prices are in it
  params: [ /* input fields */ ],
  build(p, k) { return { /* the model */ }; },
};
```

## Units

- The model is always millimetres, kilograms and newtons. The page's mm / in switch only changes how numbers print, so stock never depends on it.
- Imperial (only when asked): `units: 'imperial'`, imperial stock (`squareTube(inch(1.5), inch(0.083))`, `stockLen: feet(20)`), round inch defaults and limits (`inch(60)`).
- Every size in any text goes through `k.u`: `u.len(v)` (bare, for tables and drawings: `1500` or `59 1/16"`), `u.len(v, { u: true })` (with its unit, for sentences), `u.fine(v, { u: true })` (to a tenth: clearances, walls), `u.drill(v, { u: true })` (a drill: `8.5 mm`, `11/32"`), `u.size(v)` (overall: `1.50 m`, `4' 11"`), `u.mass(kg)` (grams or ounces when small), `u.tol(mm)` (`±1 mm`), `u.force(N)`, `u.torque(N·m)`, `u.speed(m/s)` (`10 m/s`, `22 mph`). In a table or on a drawing a bare `u.len(v)`; in a sentence always `{ u: true }`, so the number never stands without its unit. That covers tasks, checks, facts, notes, hints, option labels and `tolerance`. The audit fails "mm" left in imperial and inch marks left in metric.
- Bought things keep their trade names in either unit system: hardware names and specs, stock labels as sold (`'1-1/2" × 1-1/2" × 11 ga square tube'`), and thread or pipe sizes in any text (`1/2"-13`, `#10-24`, `3/4" NPT`, `M8`). The lint and the units capture leave those alone; every other size follows `u`.
- A shared link carries the params in the hash, always in mm and kg, bools `1`/`0`, a choice by its `value` as written: `#length=1828.8&shelf=0&top=steel` (the same for `--hash` and `audit --at`). Imperial fields show and take fractions (`59 1/16`).

## params: the input fields

```js
{ id: 'length', label: 'Length', type: 'len', value: 1500, min: 900, max: 2400, group: 'Size', hint: 'top, end to end' }
```

| type | value | the field |
|---|---|---|
| `len` | mm | mm or inches, by the units switch |
| `kg` | kg | kg or lb |
| `count` | an integer | a number |
| `number` | a plain number (`unit: '°'`) | a number with its unit |
| `choice` | one of `options: [{ value: 'steel', label: u => `${u.len(5, { u: true })} steel plate` }]` | a select |
| `bool` | true / false | a checkbox |

- `min` / `max` may be functions of the params declared **before**: `max: p => Math.floor((p.height - 270) / 250) + 1`. A limit that reads a later field stops the build with an error naming it: move the field it reads up.
- `hint` and option `label` are strings, or functions of `u` when they name a size.
- `group` puts fields under a heading (Size, Load, Options). Overall size first, unless a limit needs another field above it.
- Params are plain data outside `build`; for imperial define helpers at the top of the file: `const inch = v => v * 25.4, lb = v => v / 2.2046;`.

## build(p, k)

`p` holds the resolved params (clamped, counts rounded). `k` holds:

| name | use |
|---|---|
| `k.u` | units, above |
| `k.squareTube(b, t, o)`, `k.rectTube(bu, bw, t, o)`, `k.roundTube(d, t, o)`, `k.flatBar(b, t, o)`, `k.bar(bu, bw, o)`, `k.timber(bu, bw, o)`, `k.rod(d, o)`, `k.pvcPipe(d, t, o)` | stock sections. `bu` = width across (horizontal), `bw` = height. `o`: `{ id, label, short, stockLen, price (per m) or pricePerFt, material }` |
| `k.inch(v)`, `k.feet(v)` | imperial sizes in mm |
| `k.MATERIALS` | steel, stainless, aluminium (welded), aluminium-bare (bolted), timber, pvc, copper, copper-annealed, brass: `material:` in a section's `o` |
| `k.FILAMENTS` | PLA, PETG, ASA, ABS, TPU, PA |
| `k.shapes` | mesh generators, below |
| `k.v3` | vector helpers |

## The model

```js

  sections: { LEG: squareTube(40, 3, {...}), RAIL: ... },   // keys used by members[].sec
  axes: { x: ['right', 'left'], y: ['back', 'front'], z: ['top', 'bottom'] },  // names of +/- each axis
  datum: 'x from the left end of the top, y from the front edge, z up from the floor',
  nodes: { FL0: [x, y, z], ... },            // centre-line points, mm
  members: [...], plates: [...], hardware: [...],
  prints: [...],                             // references/prints.md
  consumables: [{ name: 'MIG wire, 0.8 mm', qty: '1 kg spool', note: '' }],
  tools: ['MIG welder', '...'],
  supports: [{ at: [x, y, z], fix: 'pin' }], // 'pin' (feet), 'fixed', 'roller'
  loads: [...],
  tip: { N: 300, height: 900, sf: 1.5 },     // optional; anchored: 'step 8, four M8 anchors' when fixed down; with: [{ kg, at }] for a carried mass that tips it worse
  checks: [{ name, pass, value, why }],      // the plan's own checks
  steps: [...],
  facts: [['Top', '14 steel bars', 'RHS 40×20 laid flat']],   // optional; what the fields do not already say
  join: 'weld',                              // 'weld', 'bolt', 'screw', 'glue', 'solder', 'clamp': the legend wording
  kerf: 2, trim: 10, minPiece: 32,
  tolerance: `cut ${u.tol(1)}; feed gap ${u.tol(0.5)}`,   // when the frame default does not fit
  printer: { bed: [220, 220, 250] },         // the bed the print check uses
  orderNote: 'One line above the build order.',

```

### members

```js
{ id: 'leg-FL', name: 'Leg', sec: 'LEG', pts: ['FL0', 'FL1', 'FL2'], step: 2, prio: 1 }
```

- `pts`: the centre line, first to last node. Interior nodes lie on that line: they are where other members meet it, and make this member the receiver there.
- `prio: 1`: runs past corners (legs, posts), cut flush with the outer face of the biggest member it meets; the rest butt onto its faces. Without it, two equal sections at a corner are mitred.
- `brace: true`: always butts onto the outline members, never wins a corner. `roll: 90`: a rectangular section the other way up. `cap: true`: an open end that gets a plastic cap. `loose: true`: bolted on, left out of the frame analysis. `tone`: `'hi'` (default), `'mid'`, `'lo'`, `'faint'`.
- Identical pieces share a piece mark automatically. End rails and cross rails often come out the same length: give members that will share a mark one name ("Short rail"), or the sheet prints "End rail / Cross rail".

### plates

```js
{ id: 'foot-FL', name: 'Foot plate', c: [x, y, z], s: [sx, sy, sz], step: 4,
  material: 'steel', holes: [{ at: [a, b], d: 10 }], note: 'Weld all round.', price: 1.5 }
```

- An axis-aligned box, centre `c`, size `s`; the thinnest axis is the thickness. Holes are on the two biggest axes, from the lower-left corner.
- Plates count in the overall size: keep foot plates inside the footprint, or the "Overall" grows past the length typed.
- `notch: true`: members pass through it (a lower shelf round the legs); the kit cuts, draws and dimensions the notches. Without it, that is a clash.
- `material`: plywood, mdf, timber, steel, aluminium, pvc, hdpe, acrylic, polycarbonate, copper, brass, fr4 (or `rho` in kg/mm³). `materialLabel` overrides the printed word only. `drawing: false` for sheet goods that need no drawing. `price` per piece, `tone`, `on: 'member-id'` when held by something it does not touch.
- Identical plates share a mark (P1, P2).

### hardware

```js
{ id: 'leveler', name: 'Levelling foot, M12', spec: '50 mm base, 500 kg', qty: 4, step: 6, kg: 0.2, price: 3,
  shape: [{ type: 'cyl', a: [x, y, 0], b: [x, y, 40], r: 25 }] }
```

- Anything bought. `shape` (a box `{ type: 'box', c, s }`, cylinder `{ type: 'cyl', a, b, r }`, sphere `{ type: 'sphere', c, r }`, mesh, or a list) draws it and makes it count in the floating check; `kg` adds to the mass, the analysis and the tip check (so a load that can be taken off is a load case, not hardware with `kg`); `on: 'id'` names what holds it if it does not touch it.
- What the builder already owns (the welder on a cart, the antenna on a mast, the tube a clamp grips) is hardware with `owned: true`, its `kg` and real `shape`: it shows in the 3D view and in its step as "yours", carries its weight, and stays out of Parts to buy and the overall size.
- **A fitting** (PVC tee, clamp, socket): put each pipe's nodes where the pipe really ends (the socket bottom) and give the fitting a `shape` round the joint; with `qty` above 1, one list per piece (`shape: [[run, branch], ...]`). Ends inside it read "into the tee", pipes meeting inside it are not a clash, and the analysis joins them. `examples/pvc-drying-stand` does this.
- Only a part the size of a fitting joins pipe ends: at most 6 × the pipe's size across. A long part (a cable, a hose, a strap) never joins the ends it spans; give anything else that holds pipe ends but is not a joint `fitting: false`.
- Entries with the same `name`, `spec` and `price` merge into one line with the total quantity.

### shapes

Bought parts and prints take their real shape. Beyond `box`, `cyl`, `sphere` (and for prints `tube`, `prism`), any shape is a **mesh** `{ type: 'mesh', pts, tris }`: points in mm, triangles as index triples facing outward, closed. The 3D view, drawings and prints all take it. `k.shapes` builds them:

| | |
|---|---|
| `sphere(c, r)` | a ball, a knob |
| `cone(a, b, r1, r2)` | a cone or frustum (a foot, a funnel) |
| `sweep(path, r)` | a round tube along points (a hose, a cable, a bent rail) |
| `arc(c, from, axis, deg)` | points along an arc, for `sweep` |
| `bend(c, from, axis, deg, r)` | a curved tube (an elbow body, a bent handle) |
| `elbow(c, d1, d2, z, sock, rHub, rBody)` | a pipe elbow at centre `c`, openings along `d1`, `d2` (any angle): two socket hubs and a curved body, as a list |
| `revolve(profile, a, b)` | `[[radius, height], ...]` spun about an axis (a bottle, a wheel) |
| `extrude(outline, z0, h, axis)` | a convex outline pushed out (split a concave one) |

When none fits, compute the points and triangles yourself. A PVC elbow is `elbow(...)`, never two cylinders meeting at the centre. A shape that keeps coming up belongs in `kit/shapes.mjs`.

### supports and loads

```js
supports: legs.map(n => ({ at: nodes[n], fix: 'pin' })),
loads: [
  { id: 'spread', name: 'Spread load on the top', kg: p.load, what: 'spread over the top', on: ['rail-F', 'rail-B'], sf: 2, defl: p.length / 300 },
  { id: 'corner', name: 'Point load at a corner', kg: 150, at: [[x, y, z]], sf: 2 },
  { id: 'shove', name: 'Shoved sideways', N: 400, dir: [1, 0, 0], on: ['rail-F'], sf: 2 },
]
```

- A support wherever it really bears: every foot, cap or fitting that rests on the ground, every clamp that holds it. Supports must hold the frame still in every direction, or the solver reports a mechanism. Two `pin`s on one vertical line (a mast in two clamps) leave it free to spin: make one `fixed`.
- `kg` (or `N`) on members in `on` is spread along them by length, so a long bay carries more than a short one; on points in `at` it is shared equally. `dir` defaults to down. Self weight is always added.
- A load can act off the frame (wind on an antenna above the mast top, a sign hung out from a post): give its real point in `at`. The solver puts the force on the nearest member point with the moment of its lever arm, so the base sees the right bending. Hardware with `kg` off the frame keeps its lever arm the same way. Give the load where it really acts; never work out an equivalent force by hand.
- `what` reads after the load in the check: "Yield ÷ peak stress with 150 kg *on one corner*".
- `parts: [{ on, at, kg | N, dir }, ...]` makes one case of several loads together (drag up a mast plus a load at its head).
- `sf`: required safety factor on yield. `defl`: largest movement allowed at the loaded points, mm.
- Plates are not in the analysis: put the load on the members that carry the top. `loose` members are left out but their weight still bears.

### steps

```js
{ n: 2, phase: 'Fabricate', title: 'Top frame (tack)', hours: 2, views: ['top'],
  summary: 'Optional one line.',
  tasks: ['Short imperative lines, sizes from u.', p.shelf && 'A falsy task is dropped.'],
  check: `Diagonals equal within ${u.len(2, { u: true })}.`,
  tip: 'Optional warning.' }
```

- Numbered 1, 2, 3 with no gaps; `phase` groups them; `hours` is honest time for one person; `views` picks the jig views (`'top'`, `'front'`, `'side'`).
- `{mark:member-id}` or `{mark:plate-id}` in any step text, check or plate note prints that piece's or plate's mark (A, P1); marks are assigned after `build()`, so this is the only way to write them.
- `alone: true` draws a sub-assembly on its own. `points: false` drops the point labels and joint table for parts placed by a rule; `table: { title, head, rows }` adds the step's own table instead. A column headed `✓` or listed in `ticks: [i]` gets checkboxes, `fill: [i]` gets number fields; both are saved on the device and print as boxes for a pen.
- Every member, plate, part and print has a `step`. Not modelled, so write them as tasks: holes in members, bends, copes.

### checks

```js
{ name: 'Knee room under the top', pass: clear >= 600, value: u.len(clear, { u: true }), why: 'Sit at it on a stool.' }
```

Anything the kit cannot know: a clearance, a work height, a span, an element length. The audit requires them at every size. Compare with a hair of margin where the numbers are built to meet exactly (`hole - bolt >= 0.3 - 1e-9`), or floating point fails a check that is right.

## A plan with no frame

Some things have nothing to cut: a printed clamp and a few bolts, a holder for a bought part. Leave `members` empty. The kit then skips the stock, cut list and frame checks, and the audit asks for no load cases or supports; instead the plan checks prove what it must do (the bore fits, the thinnest wall, the grip, the bolt engagement). Never add a fake member to get a frame check: it puts a cut sheet for a part nobody cuts on the page.

# 3D-printed parts

Read this when the plan has a printed part. A print is a part like any other: a step, the 3D view, the drawings, the materials list, and its files. The page builds the exact part at the current size, so a clamp follows the pipe size the person picks.

## When to print

Where a fabricated part would be fiddly or a bought one does not exist: a hub where members meet at odd angles, a saddle, clamp or clip on a pipe, a holder for a connector, switch or gland, a drilling or cutting jig, feet, caps and spacers (TPU where it should give). Never the main load path of anything heavy, stood on or hot. Prints are strong in compression and clamping, weak when layers are pulled apart.

## In the model

```js
prints: [{
  id: 'hub', name: 'Feed hub', step: 1, qty: 1,
  material: 'PETG', layer: 0.2, walls: 4, infill: 0.2, supports: false,
  bed: '+z', orient: 'top face down, socket pointing up; no supports',
  shapes: [
    { type: 'tube', a: [0, 0, z0], b: [0, 0, z1], r: 18, ri: pipeOD / 2 + 0.3 },   // socket onto the mast
    { type: 'cyl', a: [0, 0, z1], b: armEnd, r: 7 },                              // an arm
    { type: 'box', c: [0, 0, zTop], s: [40, 30, 8] },                             // a pad
    { type: 'prism', pts: [[0, 0], [30, 0], [0, 30]], z0: 0, h: 5, axis: 'z' },   // a gusset
  ],
  cuts: [
    { type: 'hole', a: armStart, b: armEnd, d: rodD + 0.4 },                      // a bore for a rod
    { type: 'box', c: [0, 0, zTop + 2], s: [20, 12, 6] },                         // a pocket
  ],
  copies: [{ rotZ: 120, about: [0, 0, 0] }],                                       // optional: the same part again
  note: 'Push the rods in until they bottom out; one M3 grub screw each.',
}]
```

- Plan coordinates (mm), so it sits where it goes.
- `shapes` are unioned; `cuts` and every `tube` bore are taken out. Solids: `box`, `cyl`, `tube`, `prism`, `sphere`, `mesh` (`k.shapes` or your own closed mesh). Cuts: `hole` (round, a to b, diameter `d`), `cyl`, `box`, `prism`.
- `prism` extrudes an outline, concave or convex: `axis: 'z'` takes `pts` as [x, y]; `'x'` as [y, z]; `'y'` as [x, z].
- Overlap solids that join by a millimetre, and run a cut 1 mm past any face it opens. A `tube` bore cuts through everything it overlaps; to stop a bore against a plate, use a `cyl` and a `hole` of the length you want.
- `bed`: the face that goes down on the bed, `'-z'` (default), `'+z'`, `'-x'`, `'+x'`, `'-y'`, `'+y'`. The STL and .scad come out turned that way, at the origin. Say the same in `orient` (the step prints it after "print it").
- `material`: PLA, PETG, ASA, ABS, TPU, PA. `infill` 0 to 1.
- `note`: one plain line under the print's files (what to do after printing: inserts, clearing strings). A warning goes in the step's `tip`.
- A print and a few bought parts with nothing to cut is a plan with no frame (`references/model.md`): no members, and plan checks prove the fit, the walls and the grip.
- A print touches what it holds (the floating check sees it); `on: 'member-id'` names a holder it does not touch.
- `copies: [{ move, rotZ, about }]`: each copy turned about a vertical axis through `about`, then moved. One STL; quantity is copies plus one (or `qty`).

## Design rules

| Rule | Value |
|---|---|
| Walls | 3 perimeters at least (1.2 mm on a 0.4 nozzle); 2.5-4 mm round a clamped or pushed-in bore |
| Pipe or rod bore | diameter + 0.3 to 0.5 (push fit); + 0.8 (sliding); a split clamp: diameter + 0.2, with a 2-3 mm slot and a bolt across it to close it |
| Bolt holes | + 0.3 (M3 3.3, M4 4.3, M5 5.3). Threads: heat-set inserts or a nut trap, not tapped plastic |
| Connector holes | SMA bulkhead 6.4; BNC 9.6; 6 mm panel jack 6.3 |
| Overhangs | 45° or less, or a chamfer; `supports: true` only when there is no way round it |
| Orientation | keep pulling or bending loads across the layers, not along the stack. A clamped socket is fine either way; pick the side without supports |
| Outdoors | ASA or PETG, 4 walls. PLA creeps and softens in the sun |
| Infill | 20%: the walls carry the load. When a plan check needs a stronger print, add walls before infill |

## Keep print time down

The rule "size each part to its job" (SKILL.md), for prints: time follows mass (the **3D prints** table, about 12 g an hour), so every gram should be doing something.

- **Compact.** Stack features over each other (a socket under the pocket or plate it carries, not beside it), so the body is one small block.
- **No deeper than the load.** A socket held by a push fit and a cross bolt needs about 0.75 × the tube's diameter (30 mm at least).
- **Walls, not solid.** The table's wall thickness and 20% infill; open up what holds nothing.
- **Read the table after every change.** A print over about 6 h, or one part taking most of the total, is the first to rethink.

Fits and walls are yours to prove: a plan check for each bore against what it takes and the thinnest clamped wall, sizes in `u.fine()`.

A clamp that grips by friction: grip force = bolt preload × number of bolts × friction (0.2 to 0.3 for a print on metal; take 0.25), and torque against turning = grip × the tube's radius. An M4 to M6 screw done up snug in a print gives about 400 to 800 N of preload; plastic creeps, so take the low end outdoors. Check the grip against the job with safety factor 2, and the flanges and bolt pull-out against the preload.

The frame solver does not analyse prints. When a print carries load (an arm, a bracket, a hook), prove it with a plan check by hand: bending stress M / Z at its root at most a quarter of the filament's strength (PLA 50, PETG 45, ASA 40, PA 60 MPa along the layers; halve it across them). If it cannot pass, it is not a print's job.

## What the kit does with it

- The 3D view, a drawing with every cut dashed and a hole table, its size on the bed, and a check that it fits the printer (`printer: { bed }`, default 220 × 220 × 250).
- The materials list's **3D prints** table: settings, filament (g) and time (h) estimates from the volume, and **.stl** / **.scad** downloads.
- The STL is built with manifold-3d: one closed, watertight solid every time. The .scad is its OpenSCAD source with the same facets. Capture proves every STL watertight at every end of every field.
- Print in the first step that needs the part: it takes hours, and the person can cut while it runs.

# Writing the build order and the steps

Read this when writing the steps. The steps are what a person reads with gloves on. Write them like an IKEA guide: short imperative lines, every number from the model, every step ends with a check you can pass or fail before you move on. Leave out anything an experienced builder can infer; teaching belongs in the guide, not the step.

## The order

One sequence fits every build: **make** each piece, **join** them loosely, **check** the whole, **fix** it for good, then **fit** what the earlier work would spoil. Each joining method has its loose and its fixed form:

| Joined by | Loose | Fixed |
|---|---|---|
| Welding | tack | weld out, in short stitches alternating sides so the heat does not pull it out of square |
| PVC solvent cement | dry fit, marked | cement, one joint at a time, in the dry-fit order |
| Glue and screws (timber) | dry fit, clamped | glue and screw |
| Bolts | snug | tighten, once it is square |
| Prints, connectors, wire | fitted | sealed or tied down after the test |

The kit's three phases follow from it:

1. **Fabricate**: cut, drill and print every piece (start prints first: they take hours and run while you cut). Build the biggest flat sub-frame first on a flat table, then join the sub-frames, then check every coordinate and diagonal before anything is fixed. Plates, tabs and feet from the real frame, last.
2. **Finish**: clean, prime, paint or oil. Fit tops, decks and sheet.
3. **Assemble**: bought parts, wiring and routing, then a gentle, staged test up to the rating (a load test, a leak test, a tune).

Never fix what you have not measured. Nothing hot, dusty or wet near a part it would spoil: paint, wood, plastic, prints and electronics come after.

## A step

```js
{ n: 2, phase: 'Fabricate', title: 'Top frame (tack)', hours: 2, views: ['top'],
  tasks: [
    'Rails (A, B) upside down on the table.',
    `Outside ${u.len(L)} × ${u.len(D, { u: true })}.`,
    'Clamp square. Tack each joint top and bottom.',
  ],
  check: `Diagonals equal ${u.tol(2)}. Flat at all four corners.`,
  tip: 'No welding until step 4.' }
```

On the page the step opens with its number big (64 px), the title and the time, with a 3D view beside the steps that follows the one being read; the tasks are numbered checkboxes; `check` prints after a circled ✓ and `tip` after a filled !. No boxes.

- **Title**: what you end up with, plus `(tack)` when nothing is welded out yet. "Top frame (tack)", "Weld out", "Feet".
- **Tasks**: two to six lines, each one action, as short as it can be and still be clear. Start with a verb or the part. Refer to pieces by mark ("Rails (A)"); the jig and the joint table show where they go, so do not repeat coordinates in prose.
- **Numbers**: only from the model, formatted with `u`. A plain count ("two screws per rail") is fine.
- **Check** (✓): a measurement with a tolerance, or a test (diagonals, plumb, level, rocks or not). It is the gate to the next step.
- **Tip** (!): a warning only: the mistake that costs the build, or a safety line. Not an explanation.
- **hours**: honest time for one competent person, not counting paint drying. The page totals them.
- **Explanations go to the guide.** These words get a `?` automatically the first time they appear in a step, opening a short explanation that links into the plan's guide: tack, weld out, mitre, diagonals, plumb, deburr, long point, datum, solvent cement, dry fit, load test, cutting plan, piece mark. Use the words; do not explain them in the task.

## Can it get there?

The model shows where each part ends up, not how it got there. Before a step fits a part, walk its path: what is already built round this spot, can the part pass it, and can a hand and a tool reach it to fasten it? A part goes in before whatever closes round it, or is sized to pass through the opening that is left. The same holds for everything that runs through the build: a cable, hose or pipe is threaded while its path is still open, with its connector on the end that can pass. When both ends carry plugs, the path needs an opening the plug fits through, or a slot open to an edge so the cable is laid in sideways.

Typical traps, all one mistake: a deck larger than the opening of a rack already welded round it; a sheet between posts tied top and bottom; a wheel on an axle welded at both ends; a plug that must go up a mast after the hub is bolted on.

If the order alone cannot solve it, change the design, and say in the step how the part goes in ("lower each deck down through the frames, the lowest first").

## Phrases that fail

- "Assemble the frame." (Which pieces, in what order, held how, checked how?)
- "Cut the legs to 850 mm." (Hard-coded: wrong as soon as someone types a new height, and wrong in inches. Use the piece mark; the cut sheet has the length.)
- "Weld everything." (In what order? A frame welded one corner at a time pulls out of square.)
- "Make sure it is square." (Measure what, to what tolerance?)
- "Tack each joint, which means a small weld that just holds it, on two faces so that it does not move." (Teaching in the step: say "Tack each joint on two faces."; the `?` explains tack.)
- "Optionally add bracing if needed." (The checks decide what is needed; the model either has the brace or does not.)
- "Screw the decks down." on a rack already welded shut round them. (How did the decks get in? See "Can it get there?" above.)
- "Run the cable down the mast." (In or on it? Where does it enter and leave, and when is the connector fitted?)
- A step that fits a part the materials list does not have, or a part on the list that no step fits. (The audit fails a part without a step.)

## Safety lines

Put them where they apply, once: eye and hand protection before the first cut; ventilation and no galvanised tube in a weld step (or grind the zinc off first); "lift with two people" for anything over about 25 kg; a gentle, staged load test in the last step.

# Structure and loads

Read this when laying out a frame. Stock sizes and material rules are in `references/materials/`. How to lay out a frame so the joint solver, the checks and a person with a saw all agree. In short: load takes the shortest path to the ground, the member that carries most runs through and the rest butt onto it, every piece is straight and square-cut, and the frame is squared before anything is fixed.

## Joints

The joint solver decides each joint from the geometry (`kit/joints.mjs`). Design so it lands on the joint you want:

| You want | Model it as |
|---|---|
| A leg that runs to the top with rails welded to its sides | leg with `prio: 1`, rails ending at the leg's centre line node. The leg is cut flush with the top of the rails; rails butt square onto its faces. |
| A rail halfway up a leg | an interior node in the leg's `pts`; the rail ends at it and butts onto the leg's face. |
| A picture-frame corner (two rails, same section, nothing else) | two members ending at the same node, no `prio`: mitred on the bisector. |
| A brace | `brace: true`, ending on nodes of the outline members. It butts with an angled cut; the cut sheet gives the marks. |
| A cross member between two rails | ends on interior nodes of the two rails: butts square onto their faces. |
| A piece that only rests or bolts on | `loose: true`, or model it as a plate / hardware. |

Rules the joint check enforces: a member never butts onto a smaller one (its edges would hang past the face), mitred pairs are the same section, no joint eats a whole member. Rules you keep yourself:

- **Centre lines meet.** Nodes are where centre lines cross. A rail that should sit flush with the top of a leg has its node at the rail's centre height; the leg's `prio` cut makes the top flush.
- **Flush tops.** For a top that sits on a frame, put every top-frame member at the same centre height and give legs `prio`. For rails of different heights, align them on top by putting each node at `top - section height / 2`.
- **Offsets are nodes too.** A shelf rail set in from the leg face is still a member between two nodes; put the nodes where the centre line really runs.
- **Same section around a rectangle** keeps every joint simple. Use a smaller section only for braces and shelf supports, and only where it lands on a face at least as big.

## Racking, braces and feet

A rectangle of tube welded at the corners resists racking only through its welded corners. For anything people push or lean on, check a sideways load (a shove of 300-500 N at the top, or 5% of the load sideways). If it fails or sways more than a few mm, add a lower rail rectangle (a shelf frame doubles as one), a back brace, or gussets. Prefer a lower frame: it is also a shelf.

Feet: a bare tube end marks floors and rocks. Use a foot plate (steel, welded under each leg, the leg's size or a little bigger) with a hole for a levelling foot or an anchor, or casters on a plate. Levelling feet are bought hardware with a `shape` so they show and carry the frame.

## Loads and safety factors

Write two load cases. The **job**: what it is for, at its rating, placed where it does most harm (the middle of the longest span, the end of a cantilever, the worst corner). The **abuse**: what a person or the weather will really do that it is not for (lean, sit, stand, shove, drop, snag, wind). Typical values:

| Thing | Job | Abuse |
|---|---|---|
| Workbench | its rated load spread over the top frame | 100-150 kg on one corner, 400 N shove sideways at the top |
| Shelf / rack | every shelf at its rated load | 5% of the total sideways, or a bump at the top |
| Table | 100 kg spread | a person sitting on one edge (100 kg at the middle of a long rail) |
| Stand / cart | its payload where it sits | payload at the worst corner; tip with a push at the top |
| Anything stood on | the person + 50% | 2 × the person at the worst point |

Wind, for anything outdoors: dynamic pressure q = 0.613 × v² (N/m², v in m/s), force = q × area × drag coefficient. Drag coefficients: a flat panel or sign face-on 1.2 to 2.0 (1.2 for a small plate, toward 2 for a long board), a round pipe 0.7 to 1.2, a square tube 2.0. Design gusts: 25 m/s sheltered, 30 to 35 m/s exposed (a roof, open ground), 40 m/s or more on the coast. A design wind is a choice field when it changes the design; otherwise say the value in the check.

When a failure is safe (a friction clamp that turns before it breaks, a breakaway pin), say so in the check and prove the unsafe failure instead: that the part does not break while it slips.

Safety factor (strength ÷ peak stress, what the checks report; strength is the yield for metals and the design stress for timber and PVC): at least 2 for furniture, benches and racks, and for things hung on them; 3 for anything a person stands on, sits on or hangs from; and never rely on the factor for lifting gear or vehicles (that is a Machine: see SKILL.md). Deflection: a work surface span/300 at its rated load; a steel shelf span/250 (wooden shelves span/600, since wood creeps: `materials/timber.md`); a rail or rack where sag only has to stay out of sight (a drying or hanging rail) span/80, with a floor of about 10 mm. The deflection the kit reports is how far the loaded member moves, frame and all (posts bending, joints turning), not only its own span sagging, so a tall, light frame can fail it with a short span.

Tip-over: add `tip: { N, height, sf: 1.5 }` for anything taller than about 1.5 × its depth, and for anything people push at height (a bench being planed or filed on). Use a realistic push: 150 N at the top of a rack; 150 N at work height for a light bench, 300 N for a bench used hard (vise work, planing). A light steel bench (40-60 kg) rarely passes 300 N free-standing: a heavy top, a wider stance, or anchoring fixes it. If it only passes anchored, fit the anchors in a step (as hardware in that step) and name it: `anchored: 'step 8, four M8 anchors'`. The audit checks that step fits anchors, bolts or screws. Say plainly in that step that it must be anchored.

The tip check counts the frame's own weight and any hardware with a `kg` (what stays on it, like a welder or an antenna): a load case can be taken off, so it is not counted, and the frame without it is the case that tips. When what it carries makes tipping worse (a tall gas bottle on a cart, a pot high on a stand), add it to the check: `tip: { N, height, sf, with: [{ kg: 60, at: [x, y, z] }] }` puts that mass at its centre for the tip check only. A light frame (PVC, aluminium, a few kg) fails any real push, so for those size the push to what really happens (a bump, 20 N at the top; wind on what hangs from it), and when it still fails, widen the stance with a plan check that ties the foot spread to the height (the drying stand: feet at least 0.75 × height), or weigh it down and say so in a step.

## Then change the size

Read the audit's "tightest" lines. To look at one size closely, `blueprint.mjs audit plans/<id>/design.mjs --at "length=800&height=1500"` prints every check there; use it on both sides of every threshold in your design (the length where a middle leg appears, the load where a section steps up). The sweeps hold every other field at its max (and min) while one field runs its range, so a threshold in your design is met at its worst. Then type the extremes into the page: longest and shortest, tallest and lowest, heaviest load. Look at the 3D model at each. A plan that passes its checks but looks wrong at an extreme (a 2.4 m bench with no centre support that sags visibly, shelves 100 mm apart) needs a design that adapts.

## Faults earlier plans were rejected for

Each broke a rule in SKILL.md. Look for the rule in your own plan, not the case.

- **A number not from the model**: a length typed into a step; a field that changed nothing, or only the 3D view and not the steps.
- **Proved at the wrong size**: a worst case between the samples, just before a threshold (the last length before a middle leg appears); a long rail that passed strength but sagged past span/300 at the longest size. Check the sizes either side of every threshold in your design.
- **A model that is not how it is made**: rails mitred into legs so the top was not one plane (legs need `prio: 1`); a brace butting onto a smaller tube; a shelf passing through legs with no notch (`notch: true`); a foot plate 1 mm under its leg, touching nothing; four marks for four identical legs because one node was 0.3 mm off (build symmetric nodes from the same numbers).
- **A part with no way in**: hardware with no step, so it was never bought; decks screwed into a rack already welded shut round them; coax taped down the outside of a hollow mast, its jack hanging beside it.
- **A part bigger than its job**: a printed hub that took 10 h, its mast socket beside the pocket instead of under it, deeper and denser than any check needed (6 h once compact).
- **Words that do not match the builder**: imperial plans with metric stock labels, or the reverse; "the short rails" where the mark covered three kinds of rail; joint ids in black text over dark members.

# Aluminium, copper and brass

Read this when a plan has aluminium, copper or brass parts: light frames, handles, antenna elements, conductors, ground rods.

## Choose the joint first

| `material` | Yield the kit uses | When |
|---|---|---|
| `aluminium-bare` (6063-T6) | 170 MPa | bolted, riveted or clamped: keeps its full strength. The default for home builds |
| `aluminium` (6061-T6, welded) | 110 MPa | welded: the metal about 25 mm each side of a weld loses roughly half its strength, and the kit checks the whole member at that |
| `copper` (half hard) | 200 MPa | rod, tube, bus bar |
| `copper-annealed` | 70 MPa | house wire and soft-drawn wire: bends easily, so support it often |
| `brass` | 250 MPa | small turned or threaded parts |

- Welding aluminium needs TIG or a spool gun and practice; most home builders cannot. Prefer bolts, rivets or printed or bought connectors, and `join: 'bolt'`.
- If it must be welded, keep welds away from where the bending is highest (mid span, the root of a cantilever), or let a bolted plate carry it.

## Stock

| | Common sizes | In code |
|---|---|---|
| Aluminium rod | 4, 6, 8, 10 mm | `rod(6, { material: 'aluminium-bare' })` |
| Aluminium tube | 8 × 1, 10 × 1, 12 × 1, 20 × 1.5, 25 × 1.5 | `roundTube(10, 1, { material: 'aluminium-bare' })` |
| Aluminium square / angle | 20 × 20 × 1.5, 25 × 25 × 2 | `squareTube(25, 2, { material: 'aluminium-bare' })` |
| Copper wire | 1.5 to 4 mm | `rod(2.5, { material: 'copper-annealed' })` |
| Copper pipe | 15 × 0.7, 22 × 0.9 | `roundTube(15, 0.7, { material: 'copper' })` |

## Design

- **Stiffness is a third of steel's**, so the same section sags three times as much: deflection usually sets the size, not strength. Go up a section, not a wall.
- **Keep dissimilar metals apart outdoors.** Aluminium touching steel, copper or brass in the wet corrodes fast. Use stainless fasteners with nylon or EPDM washers and sleeves, and seal the joint (paint, tape or a jointing compound). Never put bare aluminium on pressure-treated timber.
- **Threads in aluminium** strip easily: engage at least 1.5 × the bolt diameter, or use a through bolt and nut, a rivet nut or a thread insert.
- **Anodised or painted** for outdoors where looks matter; bare 6063 weathers to a dull grey and is fine.
- **Copper and brass outdoors** go green; that is harmless. Tin or seal soldered joints that carry RF or current outside.
- **Electrical and RF**: the structure is half the job. Put the electrical numbers in plan checks (element length from frequency, conductor size from current, clearances), formatted with `u`.

## In the steps

- Cut with a fine-tooth blade (a wood blade on a mitre saw works for aluminium; wax it), deburr every end.
- Drill with a sharp bit and cutting fluid; clamp thin tube so it does not crush.
- Solder copper clean and bright: flux, heat the work not the solder, let it cool unmoved.

| Where | Fasteners |

| Indoors, dry | zinc-plated or black |
| Outdoors | hot-dip galvanised or stainless 304 |
| Coastal, pool, pressure-treated timber | stainless 316 (or hot-dip galvanised for treated timber) |
| In aluminium | stainless, with nylon or EPDM washers and sleeves to keep the metals apart |

Mixing metals in the wet corrodes the less noble one (aluminium and zinc first), so keep fasteners and connectors of one metal or isolate them.

## In the steps

- Name each fastener by its size and length ("M8 × 25, washer each side"); the materials list has the count.
- Snug first, square the frame, then tighten fully.
- A torque value only when it matters (feet, a vise, a wheel); otherwise "tight with a spanner".

# PVC pipe and plastic sheet

Read this when a plan has PVC pipe or plastic sheet. Pipe: `pvcPipe(OD, wall)` (`material: 'pvc'`, a long-term design stress of 25 MPa because PVC creeps), `join: 'glue'`. `examples/pvc-drying-stand` is the pattern.

## Stock

| | Sizes | In code |
|---|---|---|
| PVC-U pressure pipe, metric | OD 16, 20, 25, 32, 40, 50 (PN10/16 walls about 1.5 to 3) | `pvcPipe(32, 2.4)` |
| PVC Sch 40, US | 1/2" 21.3 × 2.77, 3/4" 26.7 × 2.87, 1" 33.4 × 3.38, 1-1/4" 42.2 × 3.56 | `pvcPipe(33.4, 3.38)` |
| Plastic sheet | HDPE, acrylic, polycarbonate, FR4 | a plate, `material: 'hdpe'` etc. |

## Fittings

- Each fitting is hardware with a `shape` round its joint, and each pipe's nodes sit at the bottom of its socket, so the cut length is right. Draw an elbow with `k.shapes.elbow`, so its body curves.
- Laying length (centre to socket bottom) of equal tees and elbows, roughly: 20 mm pipe 11, 25 mm 13, 32 mm 17, 40 mm 21, 50 mm 26; socket depth about 0.6 × OD + 6. Tell the builder to measure their own fittings and adjust in the first step.
- Furniture-grade fittings (no print, smooth) look better; pressure fittings are cheaper and everywhere. Do not mix metric and US sizes.

## Design

- **Sag decides the size.** PVC is about 70 times less stiff than steel. Let the load limit follow the length and height (`max: p => ...`) or step up a pipe size; do not narrow the fields.
- **Creep**: never a sustained heavy bending load, and never anything a person stands on, sits on or hangs from. Things hung on it (clothes, parts, a light antenna) are ordinary loads at safety factor 2, applied to the 25 MPa design stress.
- **Heat**: rated at about 23 °C, much weaker by 40 °C, and soft at 60 °C. Keep it away from heaters, engines and a hot car's interior; in full sun on dark paving or a deck, paint it white or light.
- **Sun**: plain PVC goes brittle outdoors within a year or two. Paint it (an acrylic or plastic-rated paint) or buy UV-stabilised pipe, and say so in the last step.
- **Fixing it down**: a bolt through the pipe with a sleeve inside it (fasteners.md), or a bought or printed pipe clamp screwed to the floor or deck; then it is anchored for the tip check.
- **Never pressurised air or gas**: PVC shatters when it fails with stored gas. A frame only.
- **Light frames tip**: size the push to what really happens, and tie the foot spread to the height with a plan check (references/structure.md, tip-over).
- **Plastic sheet**: polycarbonate for anything that gets knocked (it bends, acrylic cracks); drill acrylic slowly with a sharp bit, holes at least 2 × the thickness from an edge, and oversize them so it can move with heat. HDPE for wet and wear, but nothing glues to it: screw or bolt it.

## In the steps

- Cut square (a pipe cutter or a mitre box), deburr inside and out, chamfer the outside edge slightly.
- Dry-fit the whole frame and mark each joint across pipe and fitting so it goes back the same way.
- Solvent weld one joint at a time: primer on pipe and socket, then cement, push fully home with a quarter turn, hold about 30 s. Handle the frame after about 2 h; load it only after the full cure time on the can (often 24 h). Ventilate; no flames.
- Joints that must come apart (storage, transport) are dry-fit with a screw or pin through, not glued.

## Design

- **Walls of 1.5 mm or more** for MIG at home; thinner burns through and distorts. Use 2 mm or more where a joint carries the load.
- **Square cuts and tight fits.** A gap over about 1 mm at a butt joint is a weak, ugly weld; the cut tolerance in the steps is ±1 mm for this reason.
- **Close every open tube end** that shows: a plastic cap (`cap: true`) or a welded plate. Open tubes collect water and rust from inside.
- **Stainless** where it lives wet or near food; it costs about 3-4 times mild steel and warps more when welded. Stainless fasteners in mild steel are fine indoors.
- **Galvanised tube**: grind the zinc back 25 mm from every weld, weld only with fume extraction or outdoors with a respirator rated for welding fume (zinc fume causes metal fume fever), then touch up with zinc-rich paint. Say it in the weld step.
- **To be hot-dip galvanised after welding**: every closed tube needs a vent and a drain hole (at the high and low corners as it hangs) or it can burst in the bath. Put the holes in the plate drawing or a task, and say "ask the galvaniser" in the step.

## In the steps

- Tack everything on a flat table first; square it while only tacked (diagonals).
- Weld out in short stitches, alternating sides and opposite corners like torquing wheel nuts, letting each area cool. Clamped until cold. Weld shrinkage pulls the frame toward the last weld.
- On thin wall, pre-set a corner about 1 mm out of square away from the weld so it pulls back true.
- Clean to bright metal before welding; degrease and prime bare steel the same day it is cleaned.
- Safety: eye, hand and skin protection for grinding and welding, no flammables near the work, a fire watch for a few minutes after.

## Design

- **Wood moves across the grain**, about 1% of its width per 4% change in moisture for flatsawn boards, almost nothing along it. A solid top over 300 mm wide is fixed at the middle of each rail and held elsewhere with slotted holes or tabletop clips. Plywood and MDF barely move: screw them anywhere.
- **Grain along the span.** Rails and solid shelves span with the grain. Plywood is stiffer and stronger along its face grain, which runs along the sheet's long side: a long, narrow shelf cut along a 2440 sheet has the grain along its length, so when it spans its depth (supported front and back) it spans across the grain. Check which way it really spans and use that column below.
- **Sheet properties** for a plate check (the kit does not analyse sheets). Design values with creep and moisture allowed for:

| Sheet | E along face grain | E across | Bending strength along | across | Density |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Softwood plywood (structural) | 7 GPa | 4 GPa | 20 MPa | 12 MPa | 550 kg/m³ |
| Birch plywood | 9 GPa | 6 GPa | 30 MPa | 20 MPa | 680 kg/m³ |
| OSB/3 | 4.5 GPa | 1.8 GPa | 15 MPa | 7 MPa | 600 kg/m³ |
| MDF | 3 GPa | 3 GPa | 12 MPa | 12 MPa | 750 kg/m³ |

  A sheet on two supports is a beam of its full width: stress = M ÷ (b t² / 6), sag = 5 w L⁴ ÷ (384 E b t³ / 12). Supported on all four sides it does better, but take two sides unless it is screwed down all round.
- **Shelves sag and creep.** Wood sags about 50% more over months under a steady load. Hold wooden shelves to span/600 at their rated load in the load case (`defl: span / 600`), or add a front edge strip on edge, which stiffens a plywood shelf several times.
- **Screws**: length about 2.5 × the piece being fixed; pilot holes always in hardwood and within 50 mm of an end or edge in softwood; at least 5 diameters from an edge and 10 from an end. Glue and screws in long grain; screws alone into end grain hold poorly, so use a block, a pocket screw or a bolt there.
- **Bolts** (coach / carriage bolts) where a joint carries a person or racks: a washer under every nut on wood.
- **Racking**: a timber frame of butt joints is a mechanism without help. Brace it: a plywood back or side screwed every 150 mm, diagonal braces, or corner blocks.
- **Outdoors**: pressure-treated timber, with hot-dip galvanised or stainless (316 near the sea or a pool) screws and brackets; plain zinc-plated screws rust out in treated wood. Keep end grain off the ground (feet or plastic pads) and seal cut ends.
- **Indoor furniture** wants dry timber (about 8-12% moisture); construction timber straight from the yard shrinks and twists, so let it sit indoors for a week first and say so in step 1.

## In the steps

- Cut to marks with the saw on the waste side; check square on the first piece, then use a stop block for identical pieces.
- Dry-fit, then glue and screw; wipe squeeze-out before it sets.
- Finish (oil, varnish or paint) after all cutting, with end grain sealed.
- Safety: dust extraction or a mask when sanding MDF, push sticks on a table saw.
